one_liner: Header-only C++17 zero-copy serializer for native structs; beats cereal ~48x serializing and ~670x deserializing flat index-linked graphs.
what_it_does: Cista++ writes C++ structs built from its own containers (cista::offset or cista::raw vector, string, unique_ptr, hash_map, variant, etc.) to a byte buffer or memory-mapped file whose layout is the in-memory layout, so deserializing gives you a T* into the buffer, not a rebuilt object. Standard-layout aggregates (up to 128 members) are reflected automatically, and classes with constructors or bases can list their fields in cista_members(); there is no IDL, macro or codegen. The API is cista::serialize(obj), which returns std::vector<uint8_t>, plus cista::deserialize<T, MODE>(buf), with mode flags for type-hash versioning, checksum, big-endian output, deep checks, or an unchecked cast. It does not drop in for cereal: there are no archives, and std:: containers must be replaced with Cista's.
how_it_is_fast: It is zero-copy: serialize copies each struct and container buffer into the output, then rewrites pointer fields as self-relative offsets, using an address-to-offset hash map to resolve pointers. In offset mode, deserialize never parses or allocates: it is one pass that checks pointer bounds and alignment or, with UNCHECKED/CAST, a reinterpret_cast of the buffer. offset::ptr is a position-independent self-relative pointer (the Boost.Interprocess offset_ptr idea), so a read-only mmap works wherever the file lands, while raw mode rewrites offsets into absolute pointers in place on load. Reflection comes from C++17 aggregate-arity detection plus structured bindings (to_tuple), and byte-swapping compiles out when host and format byte order match.
when_to_use: Large read-mostly C++ datasets (routing graphs, GIS data, game assets, lookup tables) that you want to mmap and query straight away with no parse step. Checked deserialize of a 25 MB graph took 0.165 ms, against 111 ms for cereal.
Data already laid out as flat arrays that reference each other by index, like the benchmark's 'slim' graph. Here serialize is mostly block copies (4.5 ms vs cereal's 216 ms).
Shared memory, or moving data between C++ processes built for the same pointer width, where the receiver should read fields in place.
You want a hash_map/hash_set (Swiss-table style, 8-byte SWAR control groups) that can be serialized, plus a type-hash version stamp and optional checksum, without writing a schema or adding macros.
when_not_to_use: Pointer-heavy object graphs. In the same 2021 run, the pointer-based Cista offset graph (unique_ptr nodes, ptr edges) took 659 ms to serialize and 248 ms to checked-deserialize, vs cereal's 216 ms and 111 ms. Raw mode took 650 ms and 256 ms checked; its 24.8 ms is the unchecked path.

You need other languages or schema evolution. Only C++ can read the data. The type hash detects layout changes but migrates nothing, and downward compatibility means hand-dispatching on your own version field.
Readers and writers with different pointer widths (wasm32 vs x64, Win32 vs 64-bit macOS). offset_t is intptr_t, so this only works after patching it to int64_t (issues #212, #281).

Compact wire messages. Every value takes sizeof(T) bytes, and a variant is always sized for its largest alternative (#121). The pointer-based graph came to 176 MB vs cereal's 37.8 MB. zpp_bits, in the same benchmark, matched Cista's serialize time (4.14 ms) using std containers.

Untrusted input with cyclic pointers when you won't pay for mode::DEEP_CHECK. The default check does not prove that cyclic structures have no dangling pointers, and the wiki warns that modifying deserialized untrusted data is unsafe.

integration.dependencies: none required (a single amalgamated cista.h, or a CMake INTERFACE target). Optional: fmt when CISTA_FMT is defined, xxh3 or wyhash (bundled) via CISTA_HASH, mimalloc via CISTA_USE_MIMALLOC
integration.min_toolchain: C++17. The maintainer says all features need GCC 9+ (GCC 7/8 have known issues). Users report Clang 10+ and MSVC 2017+ working. CI runs GCC 12, Clang 17 (libc++, ASan/UBSan) and current MSVC
integration.platforms: Any target whose byte order the header can detect (otherwise #error). CI covers Linux x86-64 and Windows amd64/x86. Reader and writer must share pointer width. Big-endian hosts byte-swap in place, so the buffer must be writable
integration.thread_safety: not documented. The containers have no internal locking (none in the vector/hash_storage headers read). Raw-mode or byte-swapping deserialize writes into the buffer, so deserialize once before sharing it

gotchas: deserialize returns a pointer into your buffer, so the buffer must outlive every use of it. The buffer must also be aligned: a misaligned one throws 'ptr alignment' (copy_from_potentially_unaligned handles that case), and cista_exception is thrown on any failed check.

A raw pointer that doesn't point into serialized data (not owned by a unique_ptr or an indexed container) is written as null. The only sign is a printf 'warning: dangling pointer' to stdout; nothing is thrown.

Structs are copied byte for byte, padding included. The benchmark adds explicit filler fields, and CISTA_ZERO_OUT exists to zero fresh memory. Plain aggregates also get a second per-field write pass (for endian conversion), while the 4.5 ms headline type skips it with empty serialize/deserialize overloads on its bitfield edges.

The CMake option CISTA_FMT defaults to ON and pulls in fmt headers, so builds without fmt fail unless you pass -DCISTA_FMT=OFF (CI does this). The v0.16 amalgamated header had to be regenerated for fmt breakage (#226, #264).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Cista over bitsery, YAS or struct_pack when the reader should use the data in place: mmap a big graph, hash map or asset file and query it with no decode or allocation, with every reader a C++ build of the same pointer width. The catalogued wins for those siblings (and FBE) are encode/decode round-trips of message-like objects, which fit better for compact network messages or types that must stay std::vector/std::string.
verified_claims_summary: The author's cpp-serialization-benchmark (Google Benchmark, GCC 11, Release, C++20, AMD Ryzen 9 5900X, Ubuntu 20.04, run 2021-12-18 with a CPU-scaling warning) used a 1,870-node graph stored as index-linked Cista offset 'slim' structs. It serialized in 4.5 ms vs cereal's 216 ms, checked-deserialized in 0.165 ms vs 111 ms, and did unchecked deserialize plus traverse in 66 ms vs 174 ms; traversal alone was about 67 ms for both because a std::set dominates it. The slim layout packs each edge into a 32-bit bitfield while cereal's graph uses three uint16 fields, so the 25.3 MB vs 37.8 MB size gap and the serialize time reflect the benchmark's data layout as well as the library.
status_note: Actively maintained: last commit 2026-09-25 (a bitvec fix), recent offset-container move and AMD GPU work, latest release v0.16 (2025-09-06). It is mostly one maintainer (547 commits by the author), MIT-licensed, and ships as a single header that is easy to vendor.
